## Abstract

*In preparation.* This chapter will examine how marine biogeochemical cycles — particularly dissolved oxygen, nutrient availability, and carbonate chemistry — vary geographically, and what that variation implies for the ecology of commercially and ecologically important fish populations. The analysis will integrate observational oceanographic data with population-ecology records to identify regions where biogeochemical stress may drive population-scale responses.

<!-- AUTO 2026-04-20 phase-4 -->
::: {.under-review}
The spatial extent and vertical shoaling of oxygen minimum zones (OMZs) in the eastern Pacific constitute a first-order constraint on pelagic fish distribution. Byrne et al. [-@byrne2024pacific] show using satellite telemetry that the Pacific OMZ creates a distributional boundary for shortfin mako sharks in the Eastern North Pacific, with the limit corresponding to the apex of OMZ shoaling in the North Equatorial Current; projected OMZ expansion will progressively compress suitable habitat for aerobically demanding species. Zhou et al. [-@zhou2020spatial] reconstruct bigeye tuna habitat across the Pacific and find that ENSO-driven OMZ fluctuations shift habitat hotspots: El Niño expands high-quality habitat northward while contracting the western equatorial band via oxycline depth changes. Gutiérrez-Bravo et al. [-@gutierrez2024anoxic] sample fish larvae across five oxygen levels in the Eastern Tropical North Pacific OMZ and find the anoxic core nearly devoid of larvae, forcing early stages into the thin oxygenated surface layer — a compression that tightens with OMZ expansion. At broader trophic scales, Le Grix et al. [-@legrix2023extreme] show using a global marine fish model that compound extreme ocean events (not single-driver anomalies) drive extremely low pelagic fish biomass over 78% of the global ocean, with low oxygen in the eastern equatorial Pacific emerging as a key co-driver alongside temperature and primary productivity. Xing et al. [-@xing2023mesoscale] further demonstrate that mesoscale eddies modulate fishing activity in midlatitude oceans through temperature and oxygen gradients at depth. Together, these studies establish OMZ geometry, ENSO-driven thermocline variability, and compound biogeochemical anomalies as a mechanistic bridge between ocean physics and fish population responses.
:::

<!-- AUTO 2026-04-21 phase-4 -->
::: {.under-review}
The relationship between dissolved-oxygen availability and fish distribution is not straightforwardly negative, as early models predicted. Moriarty et al. [@moriarty2020unexpected] monitored Pacific herring (*Clupea pallasii*) and Pacific hake (*Merluccius productus*) alongside their euphausiid prey in Hood Canal, Washington, during seasonal low-dissolved-oxygen episodes and found that pelagic fish abundance — especially herring — *increased* under hypoxia rather than declining, because vertical compression of both prey and predator into the oxygenated surface layer concentrates fish rather than excluding them; this result highlights that the ecological consequences of oxygen depletion depend critically on the specific predator–prey spatial-overlap geometry. Complementing this, Indivero et al. [@indivero2024threshold] develop a metabolic-index framework for the U.S. Pacific Coast that combines the Arrhenius temperature-dependence of oxygen tolerance with species-distribution monitoring data to infer physiological oxygen thresholds without dedicated laboratory experiments; applied to sablefish (*Anoplopoma fimbria*), the framework improved distributional predictions over temperature-only models, though it did not improve predictions for longspine thornyhead (*Sebastolobus altivelis*), indicating that the metabolic-index approach is species-specific. Together these studies caution against assuming a monotonic negative relationship between OMZ expansion and fish population declines, and motivate biogeochemically-aware distributional modelling that accounts for prey availability, species-specific thresholds, and three-dimensional restructuring of trophic interactions.
:::

<!-- AUTO 2026-04-23 phase-4 -->
::: {.under-review}
Three recent studies sharpen the mechanistic picture linking marine biogeochemistry to fish population dynamics in the Eastern Tropical Pacific — the region most directly coupled to ENSO-scale variability relevant to this chapter. Clarke et al. [@clarke2022pelagic] combine a physiological vulnerability index for large pelagic fishes with Eastern Tropical Pacific catch records from 1970 to 2016, demonstrating that ocean warming is the primary driver of changes in catch composition, while oxygen limitation introduces a significant breakpoint in the sea-surface-oxygen–vulnerability relationship in the Ecuador and Galápagos EEZs; the coupling of temperature and OMZ dynamics during El Niño events amplifies this vulnerability, although only the most extreme events produce detectable compositional shifts. Taboada et al. [@taboada2022bigeye] extend this mechanistic framework to bigeye tuna (*Thunnus obesus*) across the entire Pacific basin, showing that three-dimensional biogeochemical forecasts — integrating subsurface oxygen and thermal structure from an Earth system model — outperform surface-only predictors in hindcasting CPUE regime transitions; their analysis reveals four distinct biogeochemical regimes from 1960–2016, with regime switching most pronounced in the eastern Pacific where ENSO drives basin-wide column oxygen variability. Galloso et al. [@galloso2025humboldt] examine six decades of pelagic fish community data in the northern Humboldt Current System, confirming that dissolved oxygen and temperature together explain the long-term compositional shifts, with warmer and less oxygenated conditions driving higher species diversity — consistent with the hypothesis that OMZ expansion compresses and restructures habitat, reshaping community composition across interannual and decadal scales.
:::


<!-- AUTO 2026-05-13 phase-4 -->
::: {.under-review}
A Nature Reviews synthesis of ENSO teleconnection pathways to Atlantic marine ecosystems broadens the geographic framing of ENSO–fisheries mechanisms relevant to Chapter 4. [@rodriguezfonseca2025enso] document how ENSO-driven Walker Circulation adjustments propagate SST anomalies to the tropical and South Atlantic, altering nutrient upwelling, primary productivity, and recruitment success across the Atlantic basin. While Chapter 4 focuses on the eastern Pacific and Humboldt Current System, the structural parallels — ENSO-modulated thermocline depth and stratification driving biogeochemical anomalies that reorganise fish habitat — reinforce the mechanistic framework developed here. ⚠ relevance uncertain — Atlantic focus limits direct applicability; cite as global ENSO–fisheries synthesis context.
:::

## References {.unnumbered}

::: {#refs}
:::

<!-- AUTO 2026-04-30 phase-4 -->
::: {.under-review}
The coupling between ENSO variability and fish habitat availability through OMZ dynamics represents a central mechanism for Chapter 4. [@enso2025aerobic] demonstrate that ENSO mode and amplitude jointly determine aerobic habitat compression in the Southeast Pacific, while [@scott2025metabolic] show that this coupling yields predictable interannual fisheries outcomes at lead times useful for management. These findings anchor Chapter 4's framing: geographic variation in biogeochemical state (oxygen, nutrients, carbonate chemistry) shapes not just instantaneous habitat but its interannual and decadal predictability, with ENSO-driven OMZ dynamics as a primary driver.
:::

<!-- AUTO 2026-05-04 phase-4 -->
::: {.under-review}
[@galloso2025ensofish] directly quantify ENSO-phase effects on fish community structure in the northern HCS: El Niño events increase diversity via expanded warm oxygenated habitat; La Niña phases decrease diversity as OMZ shoaling restricts the shelf. The response scales with ENSO intensity, providing an empirical community-composition complement to the habitat-volume framing of [@enso2025aerobic] and the metabolic-constraint predictability of [@scott2025metabolic]. This ENSO-state → biogeochemical anomaly → fish habitat → community composition causal chain is the core mechanistic thread of Chapter 4.
:::

<!-- AUTO 2026-05-14 phase-4 -->
::: {.under-review}
The most direct observational quantification of ENSO-driven oxygen variability in the tropical Pacific provides a process-level benchmark for Chapter 4's biogeochemical framework. [@eddebbar2026enso] show that ENSO-driven O₂ variability in the tropical Pacific is governed by the net balance of vertical advection and biological consumption — with El Niño events increasing O₂ content despite reduced ventilation, because the concurrent decrease in biological productivity reduces O₂ demand more than ventilation loss reduces O₂ supply. This counterintuitive mechanism has direct implications for Chapter 4: if El Niño events expand oxygenated habitat in the eastern tropical Pacific through reduced biological drawdown rather than increased ventilation, then the habitat-volume predictions derived from temperature and salinity anomalies alone may underestimate oxygen availability during El Niño. The Eddebbar et al. framework suggests that a three-variable biogeochemical state (temperature, salinity, and biological productivity proxy) is needed to correctly attribute observed fish-distribution shifts to their physical versus biological drivers.
:::

<!-- AUTO 2026-05-17 phase-4 -->
::: {.under-review}
Ma et al. [-@ma2026omz] provide a comprehensive synthesis of the global distribution, drivers, and biogeochemical consequences of oxygen minimum zones (OMZs) under ongoing climate change, directly establishing the geographic context motivating Chapter 4. They document that ENSO-scale variability modulates OMZ intensity on interannual timescales — particularly in the eastern tropical Pacific — through its influence on upwelling strength, thermocline depth, and export-production-driven oxygen consumption [@ma2026omz]. The review further connects decadal deoxygenation trends to changes in stratification and overturning, identifying mechanisms by which large-scale physical-biogeochemical coupling translates remote climate forcing into habitat compression for pelagic fish communities. This synthesis supports Chapter 4's framing that geographic variation in OMZ extent is a primary mediator between ocean-physical drivers and fish population distribution, consistent with the observational evidence compiled in [@gutierrez2024anoxic] and the ENSO-fisheries linkages documented in [@eddebbar2026enso].
:::

<!-- AUTO 2026-05-26 phase-4 -->
::: {.under-review}
Recent modelling of the Gulf of California oxygen minimum zone demonstrates that ENSO-phase drives systematic seasonal and interannual OMZ restructuring: El Niño deepens and contracts the OMZ while La Niña promotes shoaling and lateral expansion, propagated by equatorially forced coastal-trapped waves [@herrerabecerril2025omz]. At the pan-tropical scale, OMZ edges are expanding under climate forcing with regionally asymmetric patterns, complicating projections of fish habitat loss [@delteil2026omz]. Future projections using CMIP6 ensembles suggest fish diel vertical migration depths may shift by more than 100 m by 2100 in the Pacific OMZ, with the most sensitive habitats at the OMZ flanks rather than the hypoxic core [@ditkovsky2026migration].
:::

<!-- AUTO 2026-05-27 phase-4 -->
::: {.under-review}
A 2026 study in *Global Biogeochemical Cycles* reveals that ENSO variability drives large interannual swings in nitrous oxide (N₂O) emissions from the Eastern Tropical Pacific, where the oxygen minimum zone sustains high N₂O production under low-oxygen conditions [@harri2026enso]. El Niño suppresses upwelling and deepens the thermocline, contracting the N₂O-productive OMZ volume; La Niña has the opposite effect. This adds a biogeochemical dimension to Chapter 4's central argument: ENSO-scale forcing shapes not only fish habitat and OMZ geometry but also the ocean's greenhouse-gas export, linking climate variability to biogeochemical feedbacks across the Eastern Tropical Pacific.
:::
